value.overview: The American Avocet is a striking North American shorebird with long, pale-blue legs, a slender bill that curves upward, and bold black-and-white wings. Adults in breeding plumage have a cinnamon-colored head and neck, while nonbreeding birds are grayish on the head and neck. It feeds in shallow wetlands by sweeping its bill from side to side through the water. The species belongs to the avocet and stilt family, Recurvirostridae.
value.classification: The American Avocet is Recurvirostra americana in the family Recurvirostridae and order Charadriiformes. It is one of four living avocet species and is native to North America.
value.identification: This large, elegant wader has a long, strongly upturned bill, very long blue-gray legs, and a white body marked by black wings and back. Breeding adults show a warm rusty or cinnamon head and neck; these areas become pale gray in winter. In flight, the broad black-and-white wing pattern is distinctive. It is generally taller and more boldly patterned than most other shorebirds found in Costa Rica.
value.rangeHabitat: The American Avocet breeds mainly in shallow wetlands of western and central North America, including marshes, alkaline lakes, ponds, salt ponds, and reservoirs. After breeding, many birds move to coastal lagoons, tidal mudflats, estuaries, salt ponds, rice fields, and flooded agricultural areas. In Costa Rica it is not a regular resident or breeding species; it occurs rarely or casually, mainly as a nonbreeding visitor at suitable coastal wetlands and mudflats. Records include the southern Pacific coast, including Golfo Dulce.
value.migrationStatus: A migratory species. Birds winter mainly from the southern United States through Mexico; Costa Rica lies near the southern edge of the species' irregular nonbreeding range, where it is a rare or casual visitor rather than a predictable migrant.
value.breeding: American Avocets breed during the warmer months in open areas beside shallow wetlands, often on sparsely vegetated ground, islands, mudflats, or dikes. They usually nest in loose colonies and defend the nest area aggressively. The nest is a shallow scrape lined with small amounts of vegetation, and a clutch commonly contains three or four eggs. Chicks are precocial, leaving the nest soon after hatching and able to walk and feed themselves.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of aquatic invertebrates, including beetles, water boatmen, midges, brine flies, fairy shrimp, water fleas, and amphipods. Small fish and aquatic plant seeds may also be eaten. The avocet commonly forages while wading or swimming in shallow water, sweeping its slightly open bill from side to side in a characteristic motion called scything. It also pecks at prey and probes soft mud.
value.behavior: American Avocets are social outside the breeding season and often gather in flocks with other shorebirds, especially Black-necked Stilts. They wade in shallow water, swim when necessary, and frequently rest while standing on one leg. Breeding birds use alarm calls, wing displays, and distraction behavior to deter predators from nests and young. Pairs may perform elaborate courtship displays involving splashing, running, circling, and intertwined necks.

conservation.populationTrend: Broadly stable over the long term according to North American breeding-bird monitoring, although some recent models indicate a slight range-wide decline with uncertainty.
